summary: Defines a generic way for IKEv2 to use any of several symmetric secure password authentication methods. It adds no new method, but provides a way to agree on which method to use and a common way to carry method-specific payloads. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Different ways to prove you know a password without sending it exist. This gives a shared way for two computers to pick which one to use and exchange the messages.

questions: how to negotiate secure password method
subtitle: A common framework for symmetric password authentication in IKEv2.

tldr.problem: Multiple secure password methods for IKEv2 were proposed, each using different negotiation and payload formats, making it impossible to implement multiple methods in the same system.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6467 defines a generic Notify payload for negotiating which secure password method to use during IKE_SA_INIT, and a generic GSPM payload for method-specific data in IKE_AUTH exchanges.
tldr.outcome: Multiple secure password methods can now coexist in a single IKEv2 implementation, allowing servers and routers with shared secrets to authenticate without certificates or EAP.

today: RFC 6467 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. It defines the framework used by multiple IKEv2 secure password authentication methods to negotiate and exchange authentication data, making it foundational for symmetric password-based IKE authentication in deployments without PKI.

sections.title: The Need for a Common Framework
sections.content:
IKEv2 normally uses asymmetric authentication with certificates or the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP). However, servers and routers often communicate using a symmetric shared secret, and neither wants to deploy a certificate authority or EAP backend infrastructure. The IETF IPsecME working group chartered to provide symmetric secure password methods for IKEv2, but multiple competing proposals emerged, each with its own negotiation and payload formats.

RFC 6467 solves this problem by defining a generic framework—not a new password method itself, but a way for multiple methods to coexist. The framework specifies how peers negotiate which method to use and how to exchange method-specific data without consuming scarce IKEv2 payload type numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: When two servers need to prove they know the same password, they need a way to agree on which secret password method to use and how to exchange messages. This RFC provides that common way.

sections.title: Method Negotiation During IKE_SA_INIT
sections.content:
Secure password methods modify the IKE_AUTH exchange to carry method-specific data. To avoid adding extra round trips, the negotiation of which method to use must happen during the initial IKE_SA_INIT exchange.

The initiator sends a Notify payload listing the secure password methods it supports. The responder selects exactly one method and includes it in its response. This is conveyed using a standard IKEv2 Notify message type numbered 16424 (SECURE_PASSWORD_METHODS).

Each secure password method is identified by a 16-bit IANA-assigned number. Different preprocessing variants of the same method can also be assigned separate numbers, or the method can negotiate preprocessing later. The responder knows which methods are supported based on administrative policy and the initiator's IP address.
sections.plainLanguage: When the computers start talking, the first computer lists which password methods it knows. The second computer picks one and tells the first computer which one they will use.

sections.title: Generic Secure Password Method Payload
sections.content:
During the IKE_AUTH exchange, each secure password method must send data to its peer. Rather than allocating separate IKEv2 payload type numbers for each method (which would be wasteful, as payload type numbers are scarce), RFC 6467 defines a single generic payload type 49 (GSPM payload).

The GSPM payload contains whatever data the negotiated method requires. Some methods may use payload subtypes within the data field to distinguish different message types, but this is method-specific. The framework does not prescribe the internal structure.

This approach conserves the IKEv2 payload type number space: instead of five separate payload types for five methods (a 31% increase in the allocated space), all methods share one.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of each password method getting its own message type number, they all use one shared message type. Inside that message, they can format their own data any way they want.

sections.title: IKE_AUTH Exchange Structure
sections.content:
The IKE_AUTH exchange proceeds as follows: The initiator sends an IDi payload together with identity and policy data, plus one or more GSPM payloads carrying the first method-specific message. The responder replies with IDr and GSPM payloads. If the method requires multiple round trips, additional message pairs are exchanged, each containing GSPM payloads. Finally, when authentication is complete, the initiator sends an AUTH payload (calculated to include the method-specific data) and GSPM payloads; the responder replies with AUTH, the negotiated security associations, and GSPM payloads.

The AUTH payload calculation is modified by the secure password method to include the method-specific data, but this is specified by each method's own documentation. The AUTH payload uses a new authentication method number (12) allocated for generic secure password methods, distinct from the existing authentication methods.
sections.plainLanguage: The computers exchange several messages back and forth. Each message can include the password method's data. When they agree the authentication is done, they calculate a final check that includes all the password method's data.

messages.label: IKE_SA_INIT request + N(SECURE_PASSWORD_METHODS) with list of supported methods
IKE_SA_INIT response + N(SECURE_PASSWORD_METHODS) with selected method
